source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 11 (PDF 244-272, printed 244-272); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 11 (Hydrocarbons), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Hydrocarbons are organic compounds that contain:
blocks.explanation: Hydrocarbons are a class of organic compounds that consist of only carbon and hydrogen (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbons is a class of organic compounds that consists of only carbon and hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: 2 Hydrocarbons are found in abundance in:
blocks.explanation: Hydrocarbons are abundantly found in petroleum and natural gas and are used as domestic and industrial fuels (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbons are abundantly found in petroleum and natural gas.

blocks.prompt: 3 Which hydrocarbons are especially used as the starting materials for a number of industrial products?
blocks.explanation: Unsaturated hydrocarbons, especially alkenes, are the starting materials for many industrial products (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Unsaturated hydrocarbons, especially alkenes, are used as the starting materials

blocks.prompt: 4 Aliphatic compounds can be:

options.text: open chain or cyclic, saturated or unsaturated

blocks.explanation: Aliphatic compounds may be open chain and cyclic, and saturated or unsaturated; they are the compounds that are not aromatic (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Aliphatic compounds may be open chain and cyclic, also they may be saturated or unsaturated.

blocks.prompt: 5 Cycloalkanes are classified as:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are acyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons, whereas cycloalkanes are cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons (11.1).

book_ref.quote: whereas cycloalkanes are cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons

blocks.prompt: 6 Alkenes and alkynes are:
blocks.explanation: Alkenes and alkynes are acyclic and unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes and alkynes are acyclic and unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons.

blocks.prompt: 7 Aromatic hydrocarbons are cyclic hydrocarbons that:

options.text: have a low carbon to hydrogen ratio and are open chain
contain only single bonds and are open chain
have a high carbon to hydrogen ratio and are based on benzene

blocks.explanation: Aromatic hydrocarbons are a special class of cyclic hydrocarbons with a high carbon to hydrogen ratio, based on benzene (C₆H₆) or resembling compounds (11.1).

book_ref.quote: have high carbon to hydrogen ratio and are based on benzene

blocks.prompt: 8 Toluene and phenol are derivatives of:
blocks.explanation: Benzene is the basic aromatic compound; toluene and phenol are its derivatives (11.1).

book_ref.quote: other compounds such as toluene and phenol are its derivatives

blocks.prompt: 9 The Greek word 'aroma', from which 'aromatic' comes, means:
blocks.explanation: The term aromatic comes from the Greek word 'aroma' meaning fragrant; these compounds have a characteristic odour (11.1).

book_ref.quote: The term aromatic was derived from the Greek word

blocks.prompt: 10 The general formula of alkanes is:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

blocks.prompt: 11 An alkane has 14 carbon atoms in its molecule. Its molecular formula is:
blocks.explanation: By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 14: H = 2(14) + 2 = 30, so C₁₄H₃₀ (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Methane (CH₄) is the simplest member of this family.

blocks.prompt: 12 The correct molecular formula of heptane is:
blocks.explanation: By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 7, heptane is C₇H₁₆ (the table's printed C₇H₁₀ is a misprint) (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ heptane is C₇H₁₆

blocks.prompt: 13 Which alkane is used as a propellant in products such as shaving gel?
blocks.explanation: Butane is a fuel in lighters; isobutane is used as a propellant in products such as shaving gel (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Isobutane is used as a propellant in products such as shaving gel.

blocks.prompt: 14 An alkyl group is named by:
blocks.explanation: An alkyl group is what remains after removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane; it is named by replacing -ane with -yl (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: The resulting alkyl groups are named by replacing –ane of the alkanes with –yl.

blocks.prompt: 15 The abbreviation Et– stands for the alkyl group:
blocks.explanation: Table 11.2: methyl CH₃– is Me– and ethyl CH₃–CH₂– is Et– (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 11.2 alkyl groups, their names and abbreviations

blocks.prompt: 16 The IUPAC name of the isopropyl group CH₃CH(–)CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Table 11.3 gives the isopropyl group CH₃CH(–)CH₃ the IUPAC name 1-methylethyl (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: iso-Propyl group (1-Methylethyl)

blocks.prompt: 17 The correct IUPAC name of the tert-butyl group (CH₃)₃C– is:
blocks.explanation: The longest chain from the attached carbon of (CH₃)₃C– has two carbons, so it is 1,1-dimethylethyl (book correction to Table 11.3) (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: the IUPAC name of the tert-butyl group

blocks.prompt: 18 The group CH₃CH₂CH(–)CH₃ is called:
blocks.explanation: Table 11.3: CH₃CH₂CH(–)CH₃ is the sec-butyl group, IUPAC name 1-methylpropyl (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: sec-Butyl group (1-Methylpropyl)

blocks.prompt: 19 The IUPAC name of the isobutyl group CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂– is:
blocks.explanation: Table 11.3: the isobutyl group CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂– is 2-methylpropyl (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Iso-Butyl group (2-Methylpropyl)

blocks.prompt: 20 How many different alkyl groups are listed for butane in Table 11.3?
blocks.explanation: From butane: n-butyl, sec-butyl, isobutyl and tert-butyl, i.e. four groups; more than one alkyl group is possible beyond two carbons (11.2.1).

book_ref.quote: For alkanes with more than two carbon atoms, more than one alkyl groups can be derived.

blocks.prompt: 21 In naming a branched alkane, the parent name is decided by:

options.text: the total number of carbon atoms
the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms
the chain written in a straight line

blocks.explanation: Rule 1: locate the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; it determines the parent name, even if it is bent in the formula (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Locate the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; this chain determines the parent name for the alkane.

blocks.prompt: 22 The longest chain is numbered beginning from:

options.text: the end nearest to the substituent
the end farthest from the substituent
either end, always from the left

blocks.explanation: Rule 2: number the longest chain beginning from the end nearest to the substituent (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Number the longest chain beginning from the end nearest to the substituent.

blocks.prompt: 23 The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Longest chain = 5 carbons (pentane); numbering from the end nearest the CH₃ puts it on C-2: 2-methylpentane (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: The parent name is placed last, and the substituent group, preceded by the number designating its location on the chain, is placed first.

blocks.prompt: 24 The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₂CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Longest chain = 5 carbons; methyl on C-2, ethyl on C-3; substituents are listed alphabetically (ethyl before methyl): 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: When two or more substituents are present, give each substituent a number corresponding to its location on the longest chain.

blocks.prompt: 25 While listing substituents in alphabetical order, which prefixes are ignored?

options.text: multiplying prefixes such as di and tri

blocks.explanation: Substituents are listed alphabetically (ethyl before methyl); multiplying prefixes such as di and tri are ignored (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: While deciding on alphabetical order ignored multiplying prefixes

blocks.prompt: 26 The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Chain of 5 carbons with two CH₃ groups on C-3; the number is used twice and di shows two identical groups: 3,3-dimethylpentane (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: When two substituents are present on the same carbon atom, use that number twice.

blocks.prompt: 27 Four identical substituents in a name are shown by the prefix:
blocks.explanation: Identical substituents are shown by the prefixes di, tri, tetra and so on, e.g. 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: When two or more substituents are identical, indicate this by the prefixes di, tri, tetra, and so on.

blocks.prompt: 28 When two chains of equal length compete for the parent chain, we choose the chain that has:
blocks.explanation: Rule 7: of two equal chains, choose the one with the greater number of substituents (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: When two chains of equal length compete for selection as the parent chain, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents.

blocks.prompt: 29 A hexane carries three methyl groups that can be numbered either 2,3,5 or 2,4,5. The correct name is:
blocks.explanation: Rule 8: when branching is at equal distance from both ends, choose the lower number at the first point of difference: 2,3,5 beats 2,4,5 at the second number (11.2.2).

book_ref.quote: choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference.

blocks.prompt: 30 A saturated ring of six carbon atoms is named:
blocks.explanation: Cycloalkanes are named by attaching the prefix cyclo to the name of the alkane with the same number of carbons: six carbons gives cyclohexane (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Cycloalkanes are named by attaching the prefix

blocks.prompt: 31 The hybridization of each carbon atom in an alkane is:
blocks.explanation: Each carbon in an alkane has four sp³ hybridized orbitals forming four single bonds; the shape around carbon is tetrahedral (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The carbon atom in an alkane has four sp³ hybridized orbitals

blocks.prompt: 32 The bond angle around a carbon atom in an alkane is:
blocks.explanation: Four bonding pairs around carbon repel equally, giving 109.5° bond angles (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: repel each other to form 109.5° bond angles

blocks.prompt: 33 The C–C bond length in alkanes is:
blocks.explanation: Carbon atoms in alkanes form 109.5° angles and a C–C bond length of 1.54 Å (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: bond angles and a C-C bond length of 1.54 Å

blocks.prompt: 34 The shapes of organic molecules are generally represented by:
blocks.explanation: Shapes of organic molecules are generally represented using the ball and stick formula, as in Table 11.4 (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: The shapes of organic molecules are generally represented using ball and stick formula.

blocks.prompt: 35 The molecular formula of cyclopentane is:
blocks.explanation: Cycloalkanes are CₙH₂ₙ; with five ring carbons cyclopentane is C₅H₁₀ (book correction to Table 11.5) (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Cyclopentane has five ring carbons and cycloalkanes are CₙH₂ₙ

blocks.prompt: 36 Cycloalkanes are called saturated because:

options.text: their rings contain a double bond
all ring carbon atoms are singly bonded to other atoms

blocks.explanation: Cycloalkanes are saturated: all the carbons that make up the ring are singly bonded to other atoms (11.2.3).

book_ref.quote: Cycloalkanes are also saturated, meaning that all of the carbons atoms that make up the ring are singly bonded to other atoms.

blocks.prompt: 37 At room temperature decane (C₁₀H₂₂) is a:
blocks.explanation: Pentane to heptadecane (C₅ to C₁₇) are colourless, odourless liquids; decane has 10 carbons (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: pentane to heptadecane (C₅ to C₁₇) are colourless, odourless liquids

blocks.prompt: 38 An alkane C₂₀H₄₂ is expected to be a:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes from C₁₈ onwards are colourless, odourless waxy solids (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: The higher members from C₁₈ onwards are waxy solids

blocks.prompt: 39 Alkanes are gases at room temperature when they contain:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes containing up to four carbon atoms are colourless, odourless gases (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: Alkanes containing upto four carbon atoms are colourless, odourless, gases

blocks.prompt: 40 Alkanes dissolve in:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar: insoluble in polar solvents like water, soluble in non-polar solvents such as hexane, benzene and ether (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: insoluble in polar solvents like water, but soluble in non-polar solvents

blocks.prompt: 41 Compared with butane (b.p. -0.50 °C), its branched isomer 2-methylpropane boils at:
blocks.explanation: Branched alkanes boil lower than their normal-chain isomers: butane -0.50 °C, 2-methylpropane -11.7 °C (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: The boiling points of alkanes having branched chain structures are lower than their isomeric normal chain alkanes

blocks.prompt: 42 As the molecular mass of alkanes increases, their solubility:
blocks.explanation: Boiling points, melting points and density increase with carbon number, whereas solubility decreases with increasing molecular mass (11.2.4).

book_ref.quote: whereas solubility decreases with the increase in molecular mass

blocks.text: 11.3 Reaction mechanism and modes of bond breaking

blocks.prompt: 43 A reaction mechanism is:

options.text: the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction
the heat given out in the reaction

blocks.explanation: Reaction mechanism is the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Reaction mechanism is the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction.

blocks.prompt: 44 In how many ways can a covalent bond break?
blocks.explanation: There are two ways: homolytic fission and heterolytic fission (11.3).

book_ref.quote: There are two ways in which covalent bonds can break.

blocks.prompt: 45 When a covalent bond breaks evenly, the products are:
blocks.explanation: Homolytic fission breaks the bond evenly to produce free radicals (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Homolytic fission occurs when the covalent bond breaks evenly to produce free radicals.

blocks.prompt: 46 A free radical is a species that contains:

options.text: a complete octet with no charge

blocks.explanation: A free radical contains an unpaired electron and is very reactive (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Free Radical is a species that contains an unpaired electron and is very reactive.

blocks.prompt: 47 Free radicals are extremely reactive because:

options.text: unpaired electrons tend to become paired

blocks.explanation: Free radicals are extremely reactive because of the tendency of unpaired electrons to become paired (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Free radicals are extremely reactive because of the tendency of unpaired electrons to become paired.

blocks.prompt: 48 In heterolytic fission the shared pair of electrons:

options.text: is gained by one atom only
is divided equally between the two atoms

blocks.explanation: In heterolytic fission the shared pair is gained by one atom only, giving oppositely charged ions (11.3).

book_ref.quote: the originally shared pair of electrons is gained by one atom only

blocks.prompt: 49 In mechanisms, heterolytic fission is shown by:
blocks.explanation: Heterolytic bond fission is shown by full curly arrows in mechanisms (11.3).

book_ref.quote: This bond fission is shown by full curly arrows in mechanisms.

blocks.prompt: 50 Heterolytic fission of the C–Cl bond in a chloroalkane gives:

options.text: a carbon radical and a chlorine radical
a carbocation and a chloride ion

blocks.explanation: Heterolytic fission gives ions: a carbocation and a chloride ion, not radicals (Figure 11.6) (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Heterolytic fission gives ions (a carbocation and a chloride ion), not radicals

blocks.text: 11.4 Unreactive nature of alkanes towards polar reagents

blocks.prompt: 51 The name paraffins for alkanes means:
blocks.explanation: Paraffins comes from Latin parum = little and affinis = affinity; alkanes are inert under ordinary conditions (11.4).

book_ref.quote: parum = little, affinis = affinity

blocks.prompt: 52 Under ordinary conditions alkanes are:

options.text: inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents
decolourized by bromine water at once

blocks.explanation: Alkanes are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents under ordinary conditions (11.4).

book_ref.quote: are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents under ordinary condition

blocks.prompt: 53 Using the electronegativity values given in the chapter, the difference between carbon and hydrogen is:
blocks.explanation: 2.5 - 2.1 = 0.4; this small difference makes C–H bonds almost non-polar (11.4).

book_ref.quote: The electronegativity values of carbon (2.5) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably

blocks.prompt: 54 Alkanes do not react with polar reagents mainly because their bonds are:
blocks.explanation: Bonding electrons in C–H and C–C are almost equally shared, making them nearly non-polar and generally unreactive (11.4).

book_ref.quote: the bonding electrons between C–H and C–C are equally shared making them almost non-polar and generally unreactive

blocks.prompt: 55 A sigma bond is very stable because its electrons are:

options.text: very tightly held between the nuclei
spread above and below the plane

blocks.explanation: In a sigma bond the electrons are tightly held between the nuclei; a lot of energy is needed to break it (11.4).

book_ref.quote: In a sigma bond the electrons are very tightly held between the nuclei which makes it a very stable bond.

blocks.prompt: 56 Incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons can release:
blocks.explanation: Combustion gives CO₂, a greenhouse gas; incomplete combustion can release carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate matter (11.4).

book_ref.quote: Incomplete combustion can release carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate matter

blocks.prompt: 57 Combustion and cracking of alkanes are examples of:
blocks.explanation: Under high temperature alkanes undergo thermal and catalytic reactions (combustion, cracking) and free radical substitution (11.5).

book_ref.quote: Thermal and Catalytic Reactions, e.g. Combustion and cracking

blocks.prompt: 58 Free radical substitution is the replacement of an atom or group of atoms by another through:
blocks.explanation: Free radical substitution reactions involve replacement of one atom or group by another through the free radical mechanism (11.5).

book_ref.quote: replacement of one atom, or group of atoms by another through the free radical mechanism

blocks.prompt: 59 Alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in the presence of:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in sunlight or UV light, replacing hydrogen atoms one after another (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in the presence of sunlight or UV light

blocks.prompt: 60 The extent of halogenation of an alkane depends upon:
blocks.explanation: The extent of halogenation depends upon the amount of halogen used (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The extent of halogenation depends upon the amount of halogen used.

blocks.prompt: 61 The reaction of alkanes with fluorine:

options.text: is highly violent, giving carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid

blocks.explanation: Fluorine reacts with alkanes highly violently, giving a mixture of carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Reaction of alkanes with fluorine is highly violent

blocks.prompt: 62 Iodine does not substitute alkanes directly because the reaction is:
blocks.explanation: Iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible.

blocks.prompt: 63 The order of reactivity of halogens towards alkanes is:
blocks.explanation: The order of reactivity of halogens is F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The order of reactivity of halogens is:

blocks.prompt: 64 The initiation step of free radical chlorination involves:

options.text: attack of Cl⁻ on a carbocation
removal of water from the alkane
breaking the Cl–Cl bond using energy from UV light

blocks.explanation: Initiation breaks the halogen-halogen bond with energy from UV light, giving two chlorine free radicals (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: It involves the breaking of the halogen-halogen bond using energy from the UV light.

blocks.prompt: 65 In the propagation step:

options.text: two radicals combine to end the chain
radicals attack the alkane and generate more free radicals
the halogen molecule splits in UV light

blocks.explanation: Propagation: the radicals formed first attack the alkane molecule, generating more free radicals (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: the initially formed radicals attack the alkane molecule generating more free radicals

blocks.prompt: 66 Which change is a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
blocks.explanation: Termination is the step in which two free radicals react together to form a product, e.g. methyl and chlorine radicals give chloromethane (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: in which two free radicals react together to form a product

blocks.prompt: 67 Traces of ethane found in the chlorination of methane are evidence of:
blocks.explanation: Two methyl radicals merging gives ethane (double carbons) in traces; its presence is evidence of the free radical mechanism (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: However, its presence is evident of free radical substitution mechanism.

blocks.prompt: 68 A mixture of chloroalkanes is obtained in the chlorination of methane because of the repetition of the:
blocks.explanation: By repetition of step (ii), the propagation step, a mixture of chloroalkanes is obtained (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: By repetition of step (ii), propagation step, a mixture of halogen substituted products (chloroalkanes) is obtained.

blocks.prompt: 69 If more chlorine gas is taken at the start of the chlorination of methane:

options.text: the proportion of chlorine atoms in the products is greater

blocks.explanation: The more chlorine at the start, the greater the proportion of chlorine atoms in the chloroalkane molecules formed (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The more the chlorine gas in reaction mixture to start with

blocks.prompt: 70 Trichloromethane (CHCl₃) is commonly known as:
blocks.explanation: Trichloromethane is also known as chloroform; tetrachloromethane is carbon tetrachloride (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Trichloromethane is also known as chloroform

blocks.prompt: 71 The last product of the successive chlorination of methane is:
blocks.explanation: Successive substitution goes CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄; tetrachloromethane is carbon tetrachloride (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: tetrachloromethane is also known as carbon tetrachloride

blocks.prompt: 72 The anaesthetic power of a haloalkane:

options.text: decreases with the number of halogen atoms
increases with the number of halogen atoms
does not depend on halogen atoms

blocks.explanation: Haloalkanes are anaesthetic; the anaesthetic power increases with the number of halogen atoms (11.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The anesthetic power of a haloalkane increases with the number of halogen atoms.

blocks.prompt: 73 Unsaturated hydrocarbons are compounds of carbon and hydrogen whose molecules contain:

options.text: carbon to carbon double (or triple) bonds

blocks.explanation: Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain carbon to carbon double (or triple) bonds; alkenes are unsaturated (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: unsaturated hydrocarbons are compounds of hydrogen and carbon only whose molecules contain carbon to carbon double bonds

blocks.prompt: 74 An alkene with five carbon atoms contains how many hydrogen atoms?
blocks.explanation: The alkane C₅H₁₂ has 2(5) + 2 = 12 H; the alkene has two hydrogen atoms less: 10 (C₅H₁₀) (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding saturated hydrocarbons.

blocks.prompt: 75 For naming an alkene, the parent chain is the longest continuous chain that:

options.text: has the most branches, whether or not it has C=C
ends at a CH₃ group on both sides

blocks.explanation: Rule 1 for alkenes: select the longest continuous chain that contains the C=C, and change -ane to -ene (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Select the longest continuous chain that contains the C = C as the parent chain.

blocks.prompt: 76 The chain of an alkene is numbered from the end:
blocks.explanation: Number the chain so that it includes both double-bond carbons, beginning from the end nearer to the double bond (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Numbering begins from the end nearer to the double bond.

blocks.prompt: 77 The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Six-carbon chain, numbered from the double bond end; the first double-bond carbon is C-1: 1-hexene (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Designate the location of the double bond by using the number of the first atom of the double bond as a prefix.

blocks.prompt: 78 The IUPAC name of H₃C–CH(CH₃)–CH=CH–CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Numbering from the end nearer to C=C: the double bond starts at C-2 and CH₃ is on C-4: 4-methyl-2-pentene (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Indicate the locations of the substituent groups by the numbers of the carbon atoms to which they are attached.

blocks.prompt: 79 A hydrocarbon whose parent chain contains three C=C double bonds is called an:
blocks.explanation: With more than one double bond: two gives an alkadiene, three an alkatriene, and so on (11.6.1).

book_ref.quote: they are alkadienes for two, alkatrienes for three and so on

blocks.prompt: 80 Reactions in which small atoms (H, OH, X) are removed from adjacent carbons to create a double bond are called:
blocks.explanation: Alkenes are prepared by removing small atoms from adjacent carbons; these are elimination reactions (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: These reactions are known as elimination reactions.

blocks.prompt: 81 Ethene is prepared from ethanol by heating it with:
blocks.explanation: Ethene is prepared by heating ethanol with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 180°C; water is removed (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: heating a mixture of ethanol and excess of concentrated sulphuric acid at 180°C

blocks.prompt: 82 In the dehydration of ethanol by H₂SO₄, the intermediate that decomposes on heating to give ethene is:
blocks.explanation: First ethyl hydrogen sulphate forms; it decomposes on heating to ethene and regenerates H₂SO₄ (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: In the first step, ethyl hydrogen sulphate is formed which decomposes on heating to produce ethene.

blocks.prompt: 83 Ethene is formed from ethyl bromide by heating it with:
blocks.explanation: On heating ethyl bromide with alcoholic KOH, ethene is formed (dehydrohalogenation) (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: On heating, ethyl bromide with alcoholic KOH, ethene is formed.

blocks.prompt: 84 Besides ethene, the products of heating ethyl bromide with alcoholic KOH are:
blocks.explanation: H₃C–CH₂–Br + KOH(alcoholic) → H₂C=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O; H and Br are removed from adjacent carbons (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: Removal of hydrogen and halogen takes place from adjacent carbon atoms to create a double bond.

blocks.prompt: 85 At room temperature an alkene with eight carbon atoms is a:
blocks.explanation: Ethene, propene and butene are gases; C₅ to C₁₅ alkenes are liquids; higher members are solids (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: C₅ to C₁₅ are liquids and the higher members are solids

blocks.prompt: 86 Alkenes burn with:
blocks.explanation: Alkenes have a characteristic smell and burn with a luminous flame (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: They have characteristic smell and burn with luminous flame.

blocks.prompt: 87 Alkenes are:

options.text: soluble in water but insoluble in alcohol
soluble in both water and alcohol
insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol

blocks.explanation: Alkenes are insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: They are insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 88 Unlike alkanes, alkenes show weakly polar properties because of:
blocks.explanation: Unlike alkanes, alkenes show weakly polar properties because of sp² hybridization (11.6.2).

book_ref.quote: they show weakly polar properties because of sp² hybridization

blocks.prompt: 89 Each carbon atom in ethene is:
blocks.explanation: Each carbon in ethene is sp² hybridized, forming three equivalent sp² orbitals in one plane (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Each carbon atom in ethene is sp² hybridized

blocks.prompt: 90 The sp² orbitals of carbon in ethene are formed by mixing:
blocks.explanation: sp² orbitals form by mixing the 2s orbital with two 2p orbitals, leaving one unhybrid p orbital (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: These sp² orbitals are formed by mixing of the 2s orbital with two 2p orbitals

blocks.prompt: 91 The angle between the unhybrid p-orbital and the plane of the sp² hybrid orbitals in ethene is:
blocks.explanation: The unhybrid p-orbital lies perpendicular (90°) to the plane of the hybrid orbitals (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The unhybrid p-orbital lies perpendicular (90º) to the plane of hybrid orbitals

blocks.prompt: 92 In ethene, the carbon-carbon σ bond is formed by:
blocks.explanation: Each carbon uses two sp² orbitals for C–H bonds; the remaining sp² orbital forms the C–C σ bond by linear overlap (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The remaining sp² orbital on each carbon is used to form a carbon-carbon σ bond by linear overlap

blocks.prompt: 93 A π bond is formed by:

options.text: overlap of s and p orbitals end to end

blocks.explanation: The parallel unhybrid p-orbitals overlap laterally to form the π bond (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: This bond formed by the lateral overlap of p-orbitals is called a π bond.

blocks.prompt: 94 In ethene, how many atoms lie in the same plane?
blocks.explanation: The two double-bond carbons and the four atoms attached directly to them (2 + 4 = 6) lie in the same plane (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The two carbon atoms forming a double bond and the four atoms attached directly to them lie in the same plane.

blocks.prompt: 95 The bond angles around each carbon in ethene are about:
blocks.explanation: sp² hybridization gives a trigonal planar arrangement with bond angles of about 120° (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The bond angles are approximately 120º, leading to a planar molecule

blocks.prompt: 96 The natural ripening hormone produced by plants is:
blocks.explanation: Plants produce ethene as a natural ripening hormone; unripe fruits are exposed to ethene (book correction: not ethane) (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Plants produce ethene as a natural ripening hormone.

blocks.prompt: 97 A π bond is weaker than a σ bond because the π electrons are:

options.text: exactly on the line joining the nuclei
away from the line joining the two nuclei, so less firmly held

blocks.explanation: π electrons are likely found away from the internuclear line, so they are less firmly held; π is weaker than σ (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The probability of finding electron is away from the line joining the two nuclei.

blocks.prompt: 98 The loosely held, exposed π electrons make alkenes undergo easily:
blocks.explanation: The loosely held π electrons are exposed to electrophiles, so alkenes undergo electrophilic addition very easily (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes, therefore, undergo electrophilic addition reactions very easily.

blocks.prompt: 99 An electrophile is a species that acts as an:
blocks.explanation: An electrophile accepts an electron pair and is shown as E⁺; a nucleophile donates a pair, Nu:⁻ (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Electrophile is a species that can act as electron pair acceptor

blocks.prompt: 100 Alkenes act as nucleophiles because they:
blocks.explanation: Alkenes act as nucleophiles because they contain π electrons that can be donated (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes act as nucleophile because they contains pi electrons.

blocks.prompt: 101 The reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through the formation of:
blocks.explanation: The reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through carbocations, so carbocation stability matters (11.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through the formation of carbocations.

blocks.prompt: 102 A carbocation is an alkyl group with:

options.text: a single positive charge on one of its carbon atoms
a double bond and no charge

blocks.explanation: A carbocation is an alkyl group with a single positive charge on one of its carbon atoms (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Carbocation is an alkyl group with a single positive charge on one of its carbon atoms.

blocks.prompt: 103 The carbocation CH₃⁺ is classified as:
blocks.explanation: A carbocation bonded to H only is the methyl carbocation (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Carbocation which is bonded to H only is named as methyl carbocation.

blocks.prompt: 104 The carbocation CH₃CH₂⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: The positive carbon in CH₃CH₂⁺ is bonded to one carbon, so it is a primary (1°) carbocation (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: If carbocation is bonded to one C or alkyl substituent then it is named as primary 1º carbocation.

blocks.prompt: 105 The carbocation (CH₃)₂CH⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: The positive carbon is bonded directly to two carbons, so (CH₃)₂CH⁺ is a secondary (2°) carbocation (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: If it is bonded to 2 carbons (alkyl substituent) directly, then it is named as secondary 2º carbocation.

blocks.prompt: 106 The inductive effect is the polarization of a:

options.text: σ bond due to adjacent electron-withdrawing or electron-donating groups

blocks.explanation: The polarization of a σ bond due to electron withdrawing or donating effect of adjacent groups or atoms is the inductive effect (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The polarization of a σ bond due to electron withdrawing or electron donating effect of adjacent groups or atoms

blocks.prompt: 107 Alkyl groups show:
blocks.explanation: Alkyl groups are slightly electron donating: a positive inductive effect (+I); halogens show -I (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Alkyl groups have a slightly electron donating Inductive effect.

blocks.prompt: 108 The correct order of carbocation stability is:
blocks.explanation: Stability rises with the number of +I alkyl groups on the positive carbon, so tertiary is most stable and methyl least (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The stability of carbocation ions increases with a number of alkyl groups due to their +I effect.

blocks.prompt: 109 A carbocation behaves as:
blocks.explanation: Due to the positive charge on carbon, a carbocation is an electrophile (11.7.2).

book_ref.quote: Due to the positive charge on the carbon atom, carbocation is electrophile.

blocks.prompt: 110 A chlorine atom attached to a carbon chain shows:
blocks.explanation: A halogen withdraws bonded electrons and displays a negative inductive effect (-I) (11.7.3).

book_ref.quote: Halogen withdraws bonded electrons from carbon to carbon bond and thus displays negative inductive effect.

blocks.prompt: 111 The -I effect of a halogen in a molecule causes:

options.text: a permanent dipole, halogen negative and carbon partial positive
a π bond between C and halogen

blocks.explanation: Electron withdrawal by a halogen gives a permanent dipole: the halogen negative and the carbon partial positive (11.7.3).

book_ref.quote: This causes a permanent dipole to arise in the molecule

blocks.prompt: 112 In a chain C₂–C₁–Cl, the partial positive charge on C₂ compared with C₁ is:

options.text: smaller (δδ⁺ on C₂, δ⁺ on C₁)

blocks.explanation: The inductive effect fades along the chain: C₂ carries a smaller positive charge (δδ⁺) than C₁ (δ⁺) (Figure 11.12) (11.7.3).

book_ref.quote: C₂ carries a smaller positive charge than C₁

blocks.prompt: 113 Which of these is listed as a minor type of reaction of alkenes?

options.text: free radical substitution in the dark

blocks.explanation: Alkenes mostly undergo electrophilic addition; minor types include oxidation, combustion and polymerization (11.8).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons and they undergo electrophilic addition reactions mostly.

blocks.prompt: 114 A reaction in which an electrophile is added to the double bond of an alkene is called:
blocks.explanation: Adding an electrophile to the double bond of an alkene is an electrophilic addition reaction (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The reactions in which an electrophile is added to the double bond of an alkene is called electrophilic addition reaction.

blocks.prompt: 115 In the generalized electrophilic addition mechanism (Figure 11.13), Y⁻ represents:
blocks.explanation: X⁺ is the electrophile and Y⁻ the nucleophile that attacks the carbocation intermediate (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: X⁺ represents an electrophile and Y⁻ represents a nucleophile

blocks.prompt: 116 The discharge of the reddish brown colour of bromine by a compound shows that the compound is:
blocks.explanation: Bromine's reddish brown colour is discharged at once by ethene; the reaction identifies unsaturation (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: This reaction is used to identify the unsaturation of an organic compound.

blocks.prompt: 117 The product of adding bromine to ethene is:
blocks.explanation: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → Br–CH₂–CH₂–Br; one Br adds to each carbon of the double bond (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: its reddish brown colour is discharged at once

blocks.prompt: 118 When a Br₂ molecule approaches the C=C of an alkene, the Br atom closest to the double bond becomes:

options.text: slightly negative and acts as a nucleophile
slightly positive and acts as an electrophile

blocks.explanation: The electron-rich double bond repels the Br–Br electron pair away, so the nearer Br is slightly positive and acts as an electrophile (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: the Br atom closest to the double bond is slightly positive and acts as an electrophile

blocks.prompt: 119 According to the chapter, the addition of bromine to ethene proceeds through a mechanism of:
blocks.explanation: Polarization of Br₂, attack by π electrons forming the carbocation, and attack of Br⁻: a three-step mechanism (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The above reaction proceeds through a three–steps mechanism

blocks.prompt: 120 In the last step of bromination of ethene, the carbocation reacts with:
blocks.explanation: The carbocation intermediate reacts with Br⁻ (nucleophile) to give the product (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: This carbocation intermediate reacts with the Br⁻ (nucleophile) to make the product.

blocks.prompt: 121 Ethene reacts with dry gaseous HBr at room temperature to give:
blocks.explanation: An alkene with a dry gaseous hydrogen halide gives a halogenoalkane: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂–Br (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: When an alkene reacts with dry gaseous hydrogen halide at room temperature, the product is a halogenoalkane.

blocks.prompt: 122 The rate of addition of hydrogen halides to alkenes is in the order:
blocks.explanation: All hydrogen halides add the same way, but the rate increases from HF to HI (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: But, the rate of reaction increases from HF to HI.

blocks.prompt: 123 When HBr adds to a symmetrical alkene such as ethene, the number of possible products is:
blocks.explanation: With a symmetrical alkene only one product is theoretically possible (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: When the alkene (e.g. ethene) is symmetrical only one product is theoretically possible.

blocks.prompt: 124 In the addition of HBr to propene, the hydrogen first adds to:

options.text: the middle carbon, giving a 1° carbocation
the double-bonded carbon with more hydrogens (the CH₂ end), giving a 2° carbocation

blocks.explanation: H adds to the double-bonded carbon with more hydrogens, creating a 2° carbocation, which Br⁻ attacks (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: hydrogen is added to double bonded carbon with more number of hydrogen, creating a 2º carbocation

blocks.prompt: 125 In the addition of HBr to propene, the minor product 1-bromopropane forms by Br⁻ attacking a:
blocks.explanation: The major product comes from the 2° carbocation; the minor product forms by attack on the primary carbocation (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The minor product is formed by the attack on primary carbocation

blocks.prompt: 126 By Markovnikov's rule, the main product of adding HCl to propene is:
blocks.explanation: The negative part (Cl) attaches to the double-bonded carbon with fewer hydrogens (C-2): CH₃–CHCl–CH₃, 2-chloropropane (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: When a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene

blocks.prompt: 127 Hydrogenation of ethene is carried out with:

options.text: H₂ and a Ni (or Pt) catalyst at 250-300 °C

blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation adds molecular hydrogen to an alkene with a Ni/Pt catalyst at 250-300 °C, giving a saturated compound (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogenation means addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene

blocks.prompt: 128 On an industrial scale, hydrogenation is used to convert:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation is used industrially to convert vegetable oil into margarine (Banaspati ghee) (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: this reaction is used to convert vegetable oil into margarine (Banaspati ghee)

blocks.prompt: 129 Gaseous ethene reacting with steam at high temperature and pressure with concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst gives:
blocks.explanation: Hydration: H₂C=CH₂ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, with H₂SO₄ as catalyst (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Gaseous alkenes react with steam at high temperature and pressure

blocks.prompt: 130 Ethene reacts with bromine in the presence of water to form:
blocks.explanation: Halohydration: H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → Br–CH₂–CH₂–OH + HBr; Br and OH go to the two carbons (book correction) (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The product is 2-bromoethanol (ethylene bromohydrin)

blocks.prompt: 131 An epoxide is:
blocks.explanation: Epoxidation of alkenes gives an oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether called an epoxide (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether called epoxide

blocks.prompt: 132 Acid hydrolysis of an epoxide gives:
blocks.explanation: Epoxides can be converted into diols by acid hydrolysis (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: The epoxides can be converted in to diols by acid hydrolysis.

blocks.prompt: 133 Ozonolysis of ethene finally gives:
blocks.explanation: Ozone cleaves the alkene oxidatively: C₂H₄ + O₃ → C₂H₄O₃ (ozonide) →(Zn/H₂O) 2CH₂O (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Ozonolysis is a method of oxidatively cleaving alkenes using ozone (O₃), a reactive allotrope of oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 134 Ozonolysis is often used to:

options.text: identify the structure of unknown alkenes

blocks.explanation: Ozonolysis breaks an unknown alkene into smaller, easily identified pieces, revealing its structure (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: This reaction is often used to identify the structure of unknown alkenes

blocks.prompt: 135 In addition polymerization, monomers with at least one C=C form:

options.text: long polymer chains as the only product

blocks.explanation: Addition polymerization: many monomers with at least one C=C form long chains of polymer as the only product (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: form long chains of polymers as the only product

blocks.prompt: 136 The monomer of PVC is:
blocks.explanation: PVC is the addition polymer of chloroethene; poly(ethene) is the polymer of ethene (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Addition polymerisation of ethene and chloroethene

blocks.prompt: 137 The repeating unit of PVC is:
blocks.explanation: The repeating unit equals the monomer with the C=C changed to a C–C single bond: CH₂=CHCl gives –CH₂–CHCl– (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: the repeating unit is the same as the monomer except that the C-C double bond is changed to a C-C single bond

blocks.prompt: 138 In the displayed formula of a polymer, the repeating unit is shown inside:
blocks.explanation: A repeating unit is represented by square brackets in the displayed and general formula (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: It is represented by square brackets in the displayed and general formula.

blocks.prompt: 139 Polyethylene, made by polymerizing ethene, is used in:
blocks.explanation: Ethene is polymerized to polyethylene, one of the most common plastics, used in bags, bottles and packaging (11.8.1).

book_ref.quote: polymerized to make polyethylene

blocks.prompt: 140 Which of the following is a conjugated diene?
blocks.explanation: In a conjugated diene the two double bonds are separated by one single bond, as in CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₃ (11.9).

book_ref.quote: In a Conjugated diene, the double bonds in the carbon chain are separated by a single bond.

blocks.prompt: 141 In a conjugated diene, the adjacent double bonds allow:

options.text: overlap of p-orbitals on three or more adjacent atoms

blocks.explanation: Adjacent double bonds allow p-orbital overlap over three or more adjacent atoms, delocalizing the electrons (11.9).

book_ref.quote: allow for the overlap of p-orbitals on three or more adjacent atoms

blocks.prompt: 142 1,3-Butadiene is used in the production of:
blocks.explanation: Conjugated dienes like 1,3-butadiene are used to make synthetic rubber; their polymer chains are rubber-like (11.9).

book_ref.quote: Conjugated dienes like 1,3-butadiene are used in the production of synthetic rubber.

blocks.prompt: 143 2-Methylbut-1,3-diene is commonly called:
blocks.explanation: The chapter gives CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂, 2-methylbut-1,3-diene, as isoprene, a conjugated diene (11.9).

book_ref.quote: Conjugated dienes and delocalization of pi electrons

blocks.prompt: 144 Isomers are compounds having:

options.text: different molecular formulas but the same structure
the same structural formula and properties
the same molar mass but different elements
the same molecular formula but different structural formulas

blocks.explanation: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas and properties (11.10).

book_ref.quote: Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural formulas and properties are said to be isomers

blocks.prompt: 145 The simplest hydrocarbon that has structural isomers is:
blocks.explanation: The simplest hydrocarbon with structural isomers is butane (C₄H₁₀) (11.10).

book_ref.quote: The simplest hydrocarbon to have structural isomers is butane (C₄H₁₀).

blocks.prompt: 146 The number of isomers of pentane (C₅H₁₂) is:
blocks.explanation: The five-carbon compound pentane has three isomers (11.10).

book_ref.quote: The five carbon compound, pentane, has three isomers.

blocks.prompt: 147 1-Chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane are isomers with the molecular formula:
blocks.explanation: Both chlorobutanes have the molecular formula C₄H₉Cl but different arrangements and physical properties (11.10).

book_ref.quote: chlorobutane molecule can have two different arrangements

blocks.prompt: 148 Structural isomerism, as described in the chapter, is exhibited in how many ways?
blocks.explanation: Chain, position, functional group isomerism, metamerism and tautomerism: five ways (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: The structural isomerism can be exhibited in five different ways.

blocks.prompt: 149 But-1-ene and but-2-ene are:
blocks.explanation: They differ only in the position of the same functional group (C=C) on the same chain: position isomerism (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: difference in the position of the same functional group on the carbon chain

blocks.prompt: 150 Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃) are:
blocks.explanation: Both are C₂H₆O but have different functional groups (alcohol and ether): functional group isomerism (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: two compounds having the same molecular formula C₂H₆O

blocks.prompt: 151 Metamerism arises due to:

options.text: shifting of a proton within the molecule
different positions of a double bond
unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group

blocks.explanation: Metamerism arises from unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group

blocks.prompt: 152 Which pair are metamers?
blocks.explanation: Ethoxyethane and methoxypropane are both C₄H₁₀O ethers differing in the carbons on each side of O (book correction: diethyl ether and methoxymethane have different formulas) (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: The printed example pair is ethoxy ethane (diethyl ether) and methoxy propane, both C₄H₁₀O.

blocks.prompt: 153 The two metamers of the ketone C₅H₁₀O are:
blocks.explanation: For the ketone C₅H₁₀O the two metamers are 2-pentanone and 3-pentanone (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: For a ketonic compound having the molecular formula C₅H₁₀O

blocks.prompt: 154 Metamers belong to:
blocks.explanation: Metamers belong to the same homologous series, e.g. both ethers or both ketones (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: Such compounds belong to the same homologous series.

blocks.prompt: 155 Tautomerism arises due to:

options.text: shifting of a proton from one atom to another in the same molecule

blocks.explanation: Tautomerism arises from a proton shifting within the same molecule, e.g. an amino acid forming a zwitterion (11.10.1).

book_ref.quote: This type of isomerism arises due to shifting of proton from one atom to another in the same molecule.

blocks.prompt: 156 Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but differ in:

options.text: the positions of identical groups in space
the length of the carbon chain

blocks.explanation: Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but differ in the positions of identical groups in space; types: geometrical (cis-trans) and optical (11.10).

book_ref.quote: differ with respect to the positions of the identical groups in space

blocks.prompt: 157 During organic oxidation, normally:

options.text: hydrogen is added or oxygen is removed
oxygen is added or hydrogen is removed

blocks.explanation: In organic oxidation oxygen is added or hydrogen removed; in reduction hydrogen is added or oxygen removed (11.11).

book_ref.quote: Normally, during organic oxidation, oxygen is added or hydrogen is removed.

blocks.prompt: 158 Organic redox reactions are characterized by:

options.text: the addition or removal of atoms/bonds
the formation of ions in water

blocks.explanation: Organic redox reactions involve organic compounds and are characterized by the addition or removal of atoms/bonds (11.11).

book_ref.quote: These reactions are characterized by the addition or removal of atoms/bonds.

blocks.prompt: 159 The conversion of ethene to ethane with H₂ over Pt is an example of:
blocks.explanation: Adding hydrogen to a C=C to form an alkane is an organic reduction reaction (11.11).

book_ref.quote: Addition of hydrogen to carbon-carbon double bond to form alkane is an example of organic reduction reaction.

blocks.prompt: 160 Which of the following is a reducing agent named in the chapter for organic synthesis?
blocks.explanation: Reducing agents used in organic synthesis include LiAlH₄, NaBH₄ and Sn + conc. HCl (11.11).

book_ref.quote: Various reducing agents are used in Organic synthesis.

blocks.prompt: 161 Which conversion is an example of reduction?
blocks.explanation: Reduction of nitriles and amides to amines, carboxylic acids to primary alcohols and nitrobenzene to phenylamine are examples of reduction (11.11).

book_ref.quote: carboxylic acid to primary alcohols, nitrobenzene to phenylamine

blocks.prompt: 162 In the complete combustion of ethane, the number of moles of O₂ needed per mole of ethane is:
blocks.explanation: C₂H₆ + 7/2 O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O: O atoms on the right = 2(2) + 3 = 7, so 7/2 = 3.5 mol O₂ (book correction) (11.11.1).

book_ref.quote: The balanced equation is C₂H₆ + 7/2 O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

blocks.prompt: 163 Oxidation of ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives:
blocks.explanation: Primary alcohols react with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to make carboxylic acids: C₂H₅OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O (11.11.1).

book_ref.quote: Reaction of primary alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to make carboxylic acids

blocks.prompt: 164 The epoxidation of an alkene is an example of:
blocks.explanation: Epoxidation of an alkene, using oxidizing agents such as molecular oxygen with metal catalysts, is an oxidation reaction (11.11.1).

book_ref.quote: The epoxidation of alkene is also example of oxidation reaction.
